name: Weston A. Price diet

lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a set of traditional-foods ideas drawn from dentist Weston A. Price's 1939 book comparing the teeth and faces of traditional and Westernised peoples. Followers connect refined sugar, flour and processed fats with dental decay and facial development.
Price's book drew early praise and later criticism for lacking quantitative analysis and controls. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.

paras: The central claim is that nutrient-dense traditional foods support normal tooth and jaw development, while processed foods cause deficiency. This is based on Price's observational comparisons, not on controlled experiments.

No specific harms were identified in the sources reviewed. Critics focus on the weak evidence base of Price's surveys and, separately, on his earlier focal infection theory, which was discredited by later reviews.

lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a "traditional foods" dietary philosophy derived from the work of Weston A. Price (1870-1948), a Canadian-born American dentist who compared the diets, teeth and facial development of traditional and Westernised populations in his 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration.[1][1] Proponents draw on it to argue that refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats lead to dental decay and narrower facial structure, themes that overlap with appearance-focused communities.

Price's nutrition work was received with both praise and criticism. Contemporary reviewers described the book as a masterpiece or as evangelistic rather than scientific, and later critics said it lacked quantitative dietary analysis and control groups.[1] The wiki found no clinical trials of a Weston A. Price diet as a whole.
infobox: Price-Pottenger Nutrition Foundation (1952); Weston A. Price Foundation (1999)[1]

paras: Price was born in Ontario in 1870, qualified in dentistry at the University of Michigan in 1893 and practised in Cleveland, Ohio. He chaired the National Dental Association between 1914 and 1928 and worked on dental radiography and porcelain furnace technology.[1]

He first studied dental disease through the lens of focal infection, arguing that infected and root-treated teeth could cause systemic illness. That theory later fell out of favour, and reviews in 1940 and 1951 criticised the methods behind it.[1] Around the 1920s he turned to nutrition, and Nutrition and Physical Degeneration (1939) compared groups including Swiss Alpine villagers, Native American, Polynesian, Pygmy and Aboriginal peoples, using many photographs.[1]

Price argued that Western diseases were rare among traditional peoples and rose as they adopted commercially processed foods, and he blamed refined flour, sugar and modern processed vegetable fats for deficiency, tooth decay and poor facial development.[1] Later organisations built dietary recommendations on these ideas; the Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig.[1]

A 1940 Canadian Medical Association Journal review called the book a masterpiece of research, and a 1950 Laryngoscope review compared Price to Charles Darwin. Other reviewers said some conclusions went beyond the evidence, and JAMA described him as observant but not wholly unbiased.[1]

A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis argued that Price held a preconceived view of primitive health, lacked quantitative dietary analysis and overlooked malnutrition, high infant mortality and gum disease. Stephen Barrett of Quackwatch likewise described Price's survey as superficial. The Weston A. Price Foundation has published a rebuttal.[1]
No studies found. The historical literature consists of Price's own observational surveys and later commentary, such as a 1950 Swiss journal article reviewing his work on diet and dental disease.[2]

timeline.event: Price graduates in dentistry from the University of Michigan.[1]
Nutrition and Physical Degeneration is published.[1]
Price dies in Santa Monica, California.[1]
The Price-Pottenger Nutrition Foundation is founded.[1]
The Weston A. Price Foundation is co-founded by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig.[1]
